This research paper focuses on two main concepts from geometry: Lie groupoids and stacks. Lie groupoids represent a non-abative generalization of Lie groups, while stacks can be seen as non-abative versions of moduli spaces. Both of these concepts have extensive uses in physics and mathematics, particularly in solving problems related to symplectic and differential structures, as well as in capturing properties of singular surfaces. Building on the principles of geometric theory, we can define geometric configurations on Lie groupoids and stacks. These configurations can preserve the groupoid's structure and are characterized by a specific morphism called descent. We can establish a one-to-one correspondence between these configurations and the geometric objects associated with the reduction of the groupoid at each point. This object reduction can be obtained through a process called geometric stack reduction. This process takes the original stack and returns a stack that contains the same information as the original stack, but is constructed from smooth components that are localized to each point. This process also allows us to generalize the concept of smooth families of Lie groups to families defined by stacks. We can further develop this concept by introducing the term "smooth family of Lie groupoids," which is equivalent to a specific type of stack. Building on this foundation, we can investigate family automorphisms and define a concept called family groupoids. These family groupoids can be realized as strict groupoids for each point, which, when combined, form a stack. This process can be further developed to investigate flat connections on stacks. These connections represent a generalization of flat connections on curves, which are essential in physics, particularly in gauge theory and Chern-Weil theory. These connections can be realized as a group of gauge transformations that is defined by the stack itself. This process allows us to capture the information of these connections on a higher level, which provides a more flexible and powerful framework for extracting topological information from a space. A statistical analysis of 64 far-infrared dark filaments, spanning a range of masses, reveals that only the most massive ones, with masses greater than 30 times that of the sun, contain infrared sources, likely because of the absence of a central luminosity source. This pattern is seen in the renowned "dark neutral gas reservoirs" throughout the Orion molecular cloud, as well as in various other molecular clouds. A model, based on mass-loss rates during the formation of low-mass stars, suggests that the core masses required to form luminous sources are generally lower than previously estimated, with a core mass of around 50 times that of the sun being sufficient to produce a luminous source. This is supported by the observation that only the most massive cores, with masses greater than 50 times that of the sun, are capable of giving birth to the most luminous sources, with outputs greater than 10 times that of the sun. This is consistent with the idea that there is a threshold mass that cores must reach before they can form massive stars, and that this threshold varies depending on factors such as the environment and the specific star being formed, rather than being a fixed quantity. This is further supported by the discovery of a similar pattern in the famous Taurus molecular cloud, as well as in the purified samples of the Orion and Taurus clouds, where the fraction of cores that are generating a luminous source decreases with increasing mass, consistent with the model's predictions. This is also seen in the celebrated TMC-1 dark cloud, which contains a famous hyper-dense core, named L1521F, with a mass greater than 50 times that of the sun, that is generating a luminous source, which is unusual because of its low optical depth, and is likely the site of a protostar, indicating that it is capable of star formation, and in the famous Bok globules, which contain a few hyper-dense cores with masses greater than 50 times that of the sun, that are generating a luminous source, and are likely the site of a pair of binary protostars, indicating that they are capable of forming multiple stars at the same time. This pattern is not seen in the famous W3(OH) dark cloud, which contains a few hyper-dense cores with masses greater than 50 times that of the sun, but that are not generating a luminous source, and are therefore capable of forming multiple stars at the same time, and in the famous G333.0-0.

This study investigates the type of one-step prediction equations known as one-step relations for spherical stochastic fields, specifically focusing on whether these equations can be optimized to minimize the mean squared error of predictions made at a given reference time. Previously established results concerning the ideal (minimum mean squared error) one-step relations under stationary and Gaussian assumptions are reviewed. Then, the focus shifts to the non-Gaussian case, where the one-step relations are derived using a generalized approach that accounts for the specific structure of spherical harmonic analysis. These derived relations enable the computation of an optimal set of one-step relations across all spatial locations, without requiring knowledge of the underlying covariance structure. Furthermore, the paper also examines the particular case of scalar stochastic fields on the sphere, providing a simple yet effective metric that can be used to assess the performance of one-step relations in a wide range of applications. The results presented in this study have been utilized in recent research involving the estimation of one-step relations for solar magnetic field stochastic fields based on historical data, with the associated code available online. The approach taken in this study can be applied to a broad range of spatiotemporal stochastic field models, including those involving nonlinear dynamics and correlated noise, with the associated code readily available for public use. Complex liquid mixtures often encounter resistance when moving through surfaces, a phenomenon influenced by surface structure, temperature, and other factors. In this study, we investigate the resistance encountered by liquid surfaces in physiological conditions, specifically focusing on the impact of rough surfaces and the underlying chemistry. To analyze this interaction, we used simple extraction chambers and compared the resistance experienced by pure surfactant liquids, as well as surfactant-coated liquid layers, on the same types of surfaces including polyethylene, glass, and air. Our findings show that the resistance of pure liquids correlates with their surface tension, whereas the resistance of surfactant-coated liquids remains constant and is unaffected by the surface's roughness or the presence of substances like protein or salt. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the resistance of these surfaces can be repurposed to separate pure liquids from coated layers based on their differing tensions, a concept we refer to as "tension-dependent trapping". Throughout this study, we also examine the theoretical underpinnings of surface interaction and propose the term "surfactometry" to describe this research. Finally, we discuss various potential applications of our discovered principles including the use of rough surfaces to enhance the purity of extracted biological samples.

The detection of cancerous cells is crucial, and doctors rely on histopathology images to diagnose skin carcinoma. However, identifying these images can be difficult and time-consuming due to the intricate details and similar appearances between cancerous and benign cells. In addition to challenges faced by medical professionals, there are also difficulties in accurately classifying images in dermatology clinics. Modern machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning, have successfully been applied to dermatology image analysis by extracting complex features from images. In this study, we employed a convolutional neural network to analyze images and incorporated a new anomaly detection method to identify unusual samples, thereby enhancing the accuracy of cancerous cell detection. We evaluated our proposed network on two datasets, namely HPA and Skin7, and the results showed that it outperformed existing models in terms of classification and anomaly detection accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed network's robustness in identifying unusual samples was validated through a series of experiments. We also incorporated a data augmentation technique to increase the proposed network's transparency by training it on augmented images. Finally, we employed a technique to visualize features detected by the network and discussed its strengths and limitations. The proposed network has significant potential applications in clinical settings, surgical operations, and biotechnology industries. The behavior of a advancing interface in a horizontal Hele-Shaw cell with rotating side walls is examined to discover how wall rotation affects interface motion and stability. Contrary to expectations, our observations reveal that increasing the rate of wall rotation leads to a transition from a stable, constant-speed interface to instability and the development of curved fingers. We determine the relevant Rayleigh number, a measure of instability driven by rotation, and calculate its rate of change for different spurring finger morphologies. When the interface is straight, a known result shows that increasing rotation accelerates the interface speed. However, once wall rotation becomes sufficient to create a system-wide centripetal acceleration greater than the force due to surface tension, the interface enters a state of instability. This occurs when the interface forms a semi-circle or we observe the development of fingering even in a cell with no initial defect. Our analyses indicate that this state of instability is driven by a balance between centrifugal force and surface tension. When a defect is present in the form of an interface with a sharp corner, the resulting spurring or fingered patterns show a stronger influence from the effects of wall rotation on the interface's rate of change than on the interface's speed. In these cases, a higher rate of wall rotation leads to a transition from a spurring interface to a fingered interface. We also examine situations where the interface accelerates to a state of stability beyond the point of marginal stability, only to be overtaken by increasing entropy and interface instability. In such cases, we observe a return to a state of marginal stability, accompanied by the development of curved fingers or the formation of sharp corners and the development of fingering. When the interface accelerates but does not reach this point, it becomes stable and moves at a constant speed. On the other hand, when the interface starts from a state of instability but does not accelerate enough to reach a state of marginal stability, it too becomes stable and moves at a constant speed. Scientists first discovered the ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecule in space, specifically in the TMC-1 cloud, through radio astronomical observations, and attributed its presence to cylic C-H=C bonds facilitating formation due to a 5-membered ring structure. Imaging technologies for human-computer interaction have the potential to link computer algorithms with human proofs and demonstrations, allowing for a more natural understanding and problem-solving. While success in this area would be significant, developing suitable methods to achieve it is challenging due to the variability and unclear underlying structures of human actions. In response to these difficulties, a new approach called "Rational Pseudocode" is proposed, which seeks to convert human demonstrations into readable pseudocodes while accounting for common ambiguities in imaging data. By representing demonstrations in this pseudocode format, their underlying logic and algorithms can be revealed and validated through normal mathematical means. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, it is applied to multiple types of algorithms, including those solved with pen and paper, and shows that in many cases, the structure of these algorithms remains accessible even after a decade. Furthermore, by examining the limitations and constraints of this method, it becomes apparent that certain algorithms cannot be derived from a single demonstration, requiring the use of multiple demonstrations to solve them. This issue is illustrated with the example of the famous Reidemeister move, for which multiple demonstrations are provided, and by analyzing its structure, it is shown that it corresponds to a specific type of algebra known as quasigroups, which is verified through direct comparison with an existing mathematical proof. This research also leads to a related problem of identifying the most minimal possible pseudocodes that can represent a given demonstration, which is shown to be equivalent to the problem of determining the minimal number of axes required to define an overlying structure, and can be solved using a simple algorithm. This approach and associated challenges are further explored through the example of the Baxter pipe dream, which is a celebrated mathematical object with an unclear and unsolved definition, and for which the method of rational pseudocode reveals a possible connection to the theory of clustered quasigroups. This research also results in a usable software tool available online for downloading. This work is an invitation to mathematicians and computer scientists to collaborate and provide guidance in order to further develop the method of rational pseudocode in order to solve the challenging problem of defining the Baxter pipe dream. This paper was originally published in the Proceedings of the 2021 ACM Conference on Human Information Interaction and Retrieval, Honolulu, HI, USA, March 2021.

This paper introduces a novel framework for dividing a stochastic pursuit-withdrawal game into multiple layers of hierarchical decision-making. Unlike traditional approaches that consider all states when defining payoff functions, our method divides the game state space into distinct levels based on the relative effectiveness of the pursuer's and evader's actions. A hierarchical model is then constructed where the pursuer and evader make decisions at different levels to maximize their expected payoff. Our research investigates a model-based reinforcement learning with system-wide performance goals in mind, and we find that learning in isolation with connected components actually results in a more robust system when individual components are suddenly compromised. In fact, this setting allows us to avert a severe system failure known as "catastrophic disruption" that occurs when a critical module is lost. We demonstrate that a modular system that learns independently can recover from disruptions by switching to a new module, achieving higher levels of performance in a range of experiments. In particular, learning in isolation with a self-tuning module proves particularly effective, recovering more efficiently from failures and producing better long-term system performance. The safety of students and faculty members depends strongly on effective virus control measures implemented in schools. While locking down classrooms and using face shields offer some level of protection, the efficacy of these methods is not well understood. To inform better infection prevention strategies, this study evaluates the reliability of two commonly used methods. The first method involves identifying whether mask coverage conforms to specifications, primarily by ensuring coverage meets a 3dp/ 120deg criterion. To determine the efficacy of mask coverage validation systems, artificial intelligence is trained on 3D models of various masks to predict their efficacy. The results show that even when masks adhere to standards, certain positions can lead to poor protection. The second method involves assessing the spread of respiratory droplets in a scenario where a student with an illness coughs in a classroom. Using computational fluid dynamics, we simulate the movement of droplets and measure the risk of virus spread to others in the room. The results show that, even with optimal ventilation designs, the risk of virus spread remains significant even at a density of 5 students per 160 square feet. To further reduce this risk, we recommend increasing ventilation rates to 15 air changes per hour. The study also examines various virus control measures, including the use of face shields. When a student wearing a face shield coughs in a classroom, the risk of virus spread to others in the room remains significant, especially in crowded rooms with poor ventilation. The study suggests that wearing a face shield alone is insufficient to prevent the spread of viruses in schools. The findings of this study highlight the importance of implementing rigorous virus control measures in schools, primarily through improved ventilation systems rather than relying solely on image-based mask evaluation and face shields. The research underlines the value of informing policies about the efficacy of virus control measures through artificial intelligence and computational fluid dynamics simulations. ViDaExpert is an application programmed in Java for visualizing and examining multidimensional data.  The tool takes advantage of a highly interactive nonlinear dimension reduction technique called t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to accurately depict high-density data regions on a two-dimensional graph.  Once t-SNE has identified the data's structure, ViDaExpert enables users to easily navigate this structure by dragging the graph's points with the mouse, thereby strengthening or weakening the connections between points in three-dimensional space.  These connections directly correlate with the probability of two data points being nearest neighbors in their high-dimensional original form.  ViDaExpert allows users to adjust the scale of the graph, remove noise data, designate specific data points of particular interest, and examine the relationship between different data groups.  The application also provides a summary of the data's organization in the form of a text file containing information about the graph's point connections and distances.  This information can be utilized to create custom versions of the ViDaExpert graph, allowing others to explore the data via the generated text file.  ViDaExpert has been successfully applied to analyze a range of complex multidimensional data sets resulting from different computational methods.
